description: We are a motivated student team passionate about space science, technology, NASA data, and innovation. Our skills include research, programming, web development, UI/UX, data analysis, visualization, and project management. We are looking for passionate team members skilled in coding, AI/ML, data science, design, research, or presentation who want to build an innovative NASA-based solution.
summary:
PROJECT X-102 is an interactive web platform created by Team Astra Intra (ASHARAB NADEEM, ABEERA MAHNOOR KIANI, ABDUL MOIZ, MISBAH ULLAH, ZAIN UL ABADIN, ABDULLAH SAJID) for the NASA Space Apps Planet X & SPHEREx challenge. It enables students, researchers, and citizen scientists to explore, align, and compare multi-epoch infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope across five scientifically distinct targets:Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

Using NASA/IPAC IRSA’s SIA2 service, our backend queries calibrated DR1 and QR3 spectral FITS files across 102 infrared channels (0.75–5.0 μm). Developed in Visual Studio Code using Python leveraging Astropy, Photutils, Reproject, and Astroquery the pipeline transforms World Coordinate System (WCS) headers to reproject multi-date observations onto a common sky grid. Users can visually inspect positional shifts via an interactive blink viewer, measure infrared flux variations, and track stellar proper motion.

To ensure scientific rigor, the platform guards against false positives caused by image misalignment, detector flags, zodiacal background light, and SPHEREx’s 6.2 arcsec/pixel resolution limits. Deployed live on Render, SPHEREx Time Explorer democratizes infrared time-domain astronomy while keeping every discovery grounded in verifiable data.
details:
PROJECT X-102 is an interactive web platform developed by Team Astra Intra (ASHARAB NADEEM, ABEERA MAHNOOR KIANI, ABDUL MOIZ, MISBAH ULLAH, ZAIN UL ABADIN, ABDULLAH SAJID) for the NASA Space Apps Challenge under the Planet X & SPHEREx challenge. It enables users to explore, compare, and scientifically analyze multi-epoch infrared observations from NASA’s SPHEREx space telescope across five distinct astronomical targets.


https://docs.google.com/presentation/d/1Vp2xEq5YSv-BXm17d8Rddtd-KfBs6HiX/edit?usp=sharing&ouid=114502248334546041435&rtpof=true&sd=true

1. What It Does & How It Works

The platform turns raw infrared sky survey archives into an accessible, scientifically verified time-domain exploration tool:

  • Target Selection & Data Retrieval: Users select from five scientifically diverse benchmark objects—Barnard’s Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis—or query specific sky coordinates (Right Ascension and Declination). Using NASA/IPAC IRSA’s Simple Image Access (SIA2) protocol, the backend retrieves calibrated spectral FITS observations from SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) and Quick Release 3 (QR3) across 102 infrared channels (0.75–5.0 μm).
  • WCS Alignment & Blink Comparison: Because raw observations are captured at different telescope orientations, dates, and detector positions, the processing pipeline uses World Coordinate System (WCS) headers to reproject and align images onto a common celestial grid. Users can visually inspect shifts using a chronological blink viewer or controlled image subtraction.
  • Astrometric & Photometric Analysis: The system tracks changes in celestial position (comparing observed pixel shifts against known stellar proper motion at SPHEREx’s 6.2 arcsec/pixel scale) and measures infrared brightness (flux and uncertainty) to generate light curves across compatible wavelength channels.

2. Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Democratizing Infrared Time-Domain Astronomy: Infrared spectral FITS cubes and multi-extension files (IMAGE, FLAGS, VARIANCE, ZODI, EPSF) are traditionally difficult for students and citizen scientists to parse. SPHEREx Time Explorer removes technical barriers by combining automated WCS alignment, metadata preservation, and interactive visual comparison in a single browser interface.
  • Scientific Literacy & Rigor: Rather than making sensational claims, the platform teaches users how real astronomers separate genuine astrophysical phenomena (like brown dwarf emission, circumstellar dust dimming, or Mira pulsations) from instrumental noise, background zodiacal light, or calibration shifts.
  • Intended Impact: To empower students, educators, and citizen scientists to actively explore NASA’s all-sky infrared survey data, fostering data driven discovery while maintaining strict scientific integrity.

3. Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Primary Programming Language (Python): We chose Python as our core backend and scientific processing language due to its rich ecosystem of specialized astronomical and data-science libraries. Key libraries used include Astropy (for FITS file handling, WCS coordinate transformations, and celestial time conversions), Photutils (for source detection and aperture photometry), Reproject (for aligning multi-epoch images onto a common celestial grid), Astroquery & PyVO (for querying NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 archives), NumPy, SciPy, and Matplotlib.
  • Code Editor & IDE (Visual Studio Code): We used VS Code as our primary development environment because of its lightweight performance, integrated terminal, intelligent code completion, and robust debugging tools which streamlined writing, testing, and running our Python data pipelines and web API scripts.
  • Web Deployment & Cloud Hosting: The interactive SPHEREx Time Explorer web application and API handler were deployed live on Render (spherex-time-explorer.onrender.com), supporting dynamic target selection, coordinate queries (RA/Dec), and spectral band filtering (e.g., SPHEREx-D3).
  • Media, Presentation & Documentation Software: CAPCUT AND GOOGLE FLOW (for generating AI-powered infrared telemetry and deep space motion sequences for our showcase video, and all editing was done on software capcut), Microsoft PowerPoint (for our 7-slide Global Judging pitch deck), and Microsoft Word (for our 10-section Scientific Guidance Report and workflow documentation).
  • Development Hardware: Built and tested on a desktop workstation equipped with an Intel Core i5 (12th Gen) processor, NVIDIA GeForce RTX 2060 GPU, and 16 GB RAM.

4. How the Project Is Creative

  • Curated Multi-Physics Benchmark Suite: Instead of focusing on a single object type, we designed the platform around five targets that each showcase a completely different physical mechanism in the infrared sky high proper motion (Barnard's Star), unresolved brown dwarf binarity (Epsilon Indi B), extreme substellar coldness at ~225–260 K (WISE 0855−0714), circumstellar dust obscuration (RW Aurigae), and long-period stellar pulsation (R Draconis).
  • Built-In Epistemic Labeling: The interface creatively separates displayed data into four transparent categories—Published Fact, Archive Observation, Calculated Result, and Scientific Interpretation so users never confuse a theoretical prediction with a direct measurement.
  • Visual Storytelling: Paired live interactive telemetry with custom false-color infrared visualizations to make invisible wavelengths intuitive to a general audience.

5. Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • False-Positive Protection: A shift or brightness change in an image does not automatically mean a new object or Planet X has been found. Our pipeline explicitly checks for 9 major error sources: image misalignment, bad detector pixels (FLAGS), cosmic-ray hits, zodiacal background variations (ZODI), incompatible wavelength channels, Point Spread Function (EPSF) differences, blended sources, detector edge effects, and data release mismatches.
  • Instrument Resolution Limits: Because SPHEREx has a pixel scale of ~6.2 arcseconds per pixel, close binaries like Epsilon Indi Ba and Bb (separated by ~0.7 arcseconds, or ~0.11 pixels) cannot be spatially resolved. Our team ensured the platform explicitly labels such targets as blended systems rather than claiming individual component resolution.
  • Data Release Compatibility & Missing Data Integrity: We standardized queries around compatible collections (DR1 and QR3) rather than mixing superseded calibrations (QR2). Furthermore, because SPHEREx’s six-month sky survey cadence does not guarantee exact six-month intervals for every coordinate, the app retrieves actual observation timestamps and displays missing dates transparently without fabricating data.
